context: A developer toolkit needs a loop-detection hook that runs after every tool invocation (file write, command execution, etc.) to detect when the AI agent is stuck repeating the same action. The hook receives a JSON event on stdin, extracts the tool name and file path, and checks against a recent-action log. The hook fires on every single tool call, so it must complete within a 50-millisecond budget to avoid perceptible lag. The toolkit is written primarily in Python and all other hooks use Python for JSON parsing.
question: Should this high-frequency hook be written in Python (consistent with other hooks) or in pure bash (faster startup)?
expert_answer: Pure bash. Python subprocess startup alone costs approximately 20ms, consuming 40% of the 50ms budget before any logic executes. Bash with lightweight JSON extraction (grep/sed) meets the latency budget comfortably.
expert_reasoning: The 50ms budget is a hard constraint driven by user experience: perceptible lag on every tool call compounds into significant slowdown. Python's subprocess startup overhead (~20ms for interpreter initialization) is a fixed cost that cannot be optimized away, leaving only 30ms for actual logic. Bash with simple string extraction avoids this overhead entirely, starting in under 2ms. The hook's logic is simple enough (extract two fields from JSON, check a log file) that bash's limitations in JSON parsing don't matter -- the input is well-structured and the extraction is mechanical. Consistency with other hooks is a weak argument when it conflicts with a hard performance constraint. The other hooks don't have the same per-invocation latency requirement.
anti_pattern: Choosing Python for consistency with other hooks or developer familiarity. This prioritizes code uniformity over the hard latency constraint. A 20ms Python startup on every tool call adds perceptible lag to every file write, every command execution, and every edit -- hundreds of times per session. The cumulative slowdown degrades the development experience for a consistency benefit that only matters when maintaining the hook code, which happens rarely.
